newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto fears vote-rigging, rival hopes to win.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto fears vote-rigging, rival hopes to win.

text.p: Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto voiced fears on Sunday of vote-rigging in Monday's general election, which her main rival Nawaz Sharif said he was confident of winning.

Bhutto said at her family village of Nuadero in the southern province of Sindh she had reports that the caretaker government planned to rig the vote in 63 constituencies of the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and that she would not accept the result if it happened.
Sharif said on Sunday that he was counting on a comfortable majority in the National Assembly.
He said tackling Pakistan's dire economic problems would be his first priority if elected prime minister.
He told Reuters in an interview in his home city of Lahore that repairing the economy would be a long, difficult task, but he was confident Pakistan could become an "Asian Tiger".
"The economy is in very bad shape because of the mismanagement of the Benazir Bhutto government," he said.

Bhutto, who received a tumultuous welcome from crowds as she drove to Naudero, told reporters that Pakistan was in "a terrible economic crisis" that only her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) could tackle.

She said she had written to Chief Election Commissioner Fakhre Alam about her fears of rigging in 48 constituencies in the central province of Punjab, 11 in Sindh and four in the North West Frontier province and asked him to stop this from happening.
Bhutto said she would not accept the result if it did not reflect the results of the 1988 and 1993 elections, which she had won. "If there is rigging, the nation will not accept the result."
Alam said his commission had made arrangements to hold fair elections and he expected a good turnout of voters.
Most commentators have predicted a low turnout after a lacklustre campaign in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
"I hope, God willing, they will be very fair, transparent and credible elections," Alam told state television.

President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on charges of corruption and misrule, but the caretaker government he appointed has failed to nail any leading politicians or bar them from standing for election.
A PPP spokesman denied a report by London's Sunday Times that Bhutto might seek asylum in Britain if she lost the poll.
"It's rubbish," the spokesman told the official APP news agency. "She has got to play a historic role in the politics of Pakistan and she will never flee the country."

The Sunday Times quoted senior Pakistani government sources as saying that corruption charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari would be dropped if she agreed to leave the country and abandon politics.
Bhutto and Zardari, who is held on a charge of conspiring in the murder of his wife's estranged brother Murtaza in September, have denied any wrongdoing, saying they are victims of a plot.

Sharif's previous government was dismissed on corruption charges but was restored by the Supreme Court, only to lose power again two months later. His Pakistan Muslim League party lost the October 1993 polls to the PPP.
Last week, the Supreme Court upheld Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto, saying there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses for him to have fired her.
Corruption has been the main issue in a campaign that has failed to excite Pakistanis, many of whom are disillusioned by the perceived misdeeds of the political class.
Imran Khan, Pakistan's former cricket captain, was the first to focus public attention on the issue, but polls suggest his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) is unlikely to win more than a few seats.
Sharif, an industrialist, promised to strengthen a commission set up by the caretaker government to root out graft.
Tension mounted in the violence-prone port city of Karachi after stone-throwing clashes between supporters of rival factions of the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM).

The mainstream MQM, led by self-exiled Altaf Hussain, expects to win a dozen seats in Karachi and could play a key role in post-election bargaining if no party gains a clear majority for any party. The MQM boycotted the 1993 polls.
